newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden says too late to stop plutonium shipment.
newsitem.headline: Sweden says too late to stop plutonium shipment.

text.p: Sweden said on Wednesday it was too late to stop a nuclear waste processing contract that will mean shipping about 900 kg (1,980 lbs) of plutonium back to Sweden from Britain despite protests from environmental groups.

Sweden shipped about 140 tonnes of nuclear waste to Sellafield, northern England between the late 1970s and 1982 for reprocessing. But it has since changed its policy and now supports storing rather than processing waste from its 12 nuclear reactors.

Until recently the Sellafield plant did not have the proper facilities to process the waste so kept it in storage, but officials now say the processing will proceed this autumn -- even though Sweden has had second thoughts.
But a Swedish investigation found it would be too dangerous -- and costly -- to break the contract and bring the waste back to Sweden untreated.
"We started an investigation to see if it was possible to bring the fuel back to Sweden but it was hazardous to test this," Swedish Environment Minister Anna Lindh told Reuters.
"We didn't want to continue the investigation as it could be hazardous to staff."

Lindh said Sweden had been left with little alternative but to allow Sellafield's operator, state-owned British Nuclear Fuels (BNFL), to go ahead and process the waste, and then bring the end product back to Sweden.
The waste was originally sent in five separate shipments as part of a private contract between Swedish power group Oskarshamns Kraftgrupp and BNFL.
But environment groups have demanded that the fuel should not be reprocessed and either stay in storage at Sellafield or be returned to Sweden unprocessed.
"The government has made a half-hearted attempt to try to take the nuclear waste back, but failed," said Greenpeace Sweden spokesman Dima Litvinov in a statement.
"Now is the last chance for Anna Lindh to act before she has to face 900 kg of deadly plutonium which nobody knows how to store."
Litvinov said the plan also contradicted Sweden's policy for non-proliferation of nuclear weapons. Reprocessing, which frees up plutonium, can be used to make weapons.
Sweden will probably opt to convert the plutonium into mixed oxide or MOX fuel, a combination of plutonium and uranium, which can fuel a nuclear plant but is not normally used in Sweden.
"It would just be an exception. We are not planning a new decision or policy," Lindh said.
Lars Hogberg, general director at the Swedish Nuclear Power Inspectorate SKI, defended the plan to process the waste in Britain, saying it would probably be less expensive and safer.
"BNFL made it clear it would not agree to breaking the contract without additional costs," Hogberg told Reuters.
No financial details of how much the contract was worth were available.
